Convenient and Captive Populations
  • Source: Beyond Consent: Seeking Justice in Research, Vol. 7 (1998)
  • Topic: Ethical use of vulnerable populations in clinical research
  • Author(s): Jonathan D. Moreno
1. Convenient & Captive Populations Defined
  • Clinical research --> complex, expensive, valued social activity
  • Convenient populations = readily available for recruitment & monitoring
  • Examples: prisoners, institutionalized persons, military personnel, students, research staff
  • Captive populations = constrained by explicit conditions formally imposed by societal decision
  • Paradigm case: imprisoned persons
  • Middle ground populations:
  • Short-term hospitalized patients
  • Long-term prisoners
  • Students, institutionalized persons, military personnel
1.1 What Makes These Populations Different
  • Greater availability for research activities
  • Higher likelihood of coercion or manipulation due to dependent status
  • Extended periods of availability --> enhanced attractiveness to research enterprise
2. Justice Across Time: Historical Overview
2.1 Prisoners
  • Most fully captive population
  • Ancient world: living criminals used in poison experiments & vivisection
  • 18th century Europe: prisoners exposed to venereal disease, cancers, typhoid, scarlet fever
  • 1914: Pellagra study using Mississippi convicts --> presaged greater use
2.1.1 World War II Era
  • Many prisoners participated in malaria & STD studies
  • Motivations: patriotism, payment, early parole
  • Nazi defense attorneys cited US prison research as justification for concentration camp experiments
  • Cited: pellagra studies, malaria studies, typhus/beriberi experiments on condemned criminals in Philippines
2.1.2 Post-WWII Developments
  • Nuremberg trial (1945-1946) --> some defendants sentenced to death, others to jail
  • Little apparent effect on US prison research conduct
  • Dr. Andrew Ivy --> authored portions of Nuremberg Code (as AMA representative)
  • Also chaired Illinois committee reviewing prison research ethics
  • Committee endorsed continued use of prisoners
  • Report published months after Nazi doctors' trial --> forestalled direct application of Nuremberg results to US prisons
2.1.3 Early Draft Declaration of Helsinki
  • Original early draft would have explicitly prohibited prison research
  • Revised at insistence of United States
2.1.4 Peak Usage (1960s)
  • Drug manufacturers invested heavily in prison research
  • Some penitentiaries built state-of-the-art laboratory facilities
  • By 1960: as many as 20,000 federal prisoners in medical experiments
  • By 1973: ~70% of Phase I drug tests on prisoners (~3600 individuals)
  • American prisons also used to test drugs for researchers abroad
2.1.5 Testicular Irradiation Study (1963-1973)
  • 131 prisoners in Oregon & Washington State penitentaries
  • Funded by: Atomic Energy Commission (AEC)
  • Clear rules existed including written consent requirement
  • 1995 ACHRE findings:
  • Rules not fully observed
  • Criticism: failure to use word "cancer" in listing risks
  • Healthy "volunteer" subjects
2.1.6 Prisoner Incentives for Participation
  • Far higher pay than other prison jobs
  • Possibility of more favorable parole status
  • Break in boredom of incarceration
  • Better food & living conditions
2.1.7 1974 Editorial Position (Journal of Legal Medicine)
  • Argued prisoners should be free to choose research participation
  • Claimed denying this opportunity was "immoral in itself"
  • Called it "an abridgment of whatever civil and constitutional rights they may possess"
  • Concluded: "biomedical research is an absolute necessity if society is to survive"
2.1.8 Mid-1970s Decline
  • 1976: National Commission recommended moratorium on prisoner experiments
  • Followed Tuskegee Syphilis Study revelations & Attica prison riot (September 1971)
  • Attica: fierce response by NY State Police --> dozens of African-American prisoners dead
  • Tuskegee + Attica exposed coercive nature of prison life
  • Moratorium met with harsh criticism from physicians, advocates, prisoners themselves
  • Louis Lasagna: condemned recommendations as destroying "properly performed research"
  • DHEW instead promulgated regulations --> effectively prohibit nearly all prison research
2.1.9 National Commission Inmate Quote
  • "It makes a prisoner feel good to volunteer. It makes him feel like he's doing something productive"
  • But Commission also heard: primary reason for volunteering was financial
  • Few opportunities to earn money for self or loved ones on outside
2.1.10 Early 1990s Federal Regulations
  • Prison research allowable only for 4 highly restricted kinds:
  • Minimal risk research on incarceration & criminal behavior
  • Studies of prisons as institutions or prisoners as incarcerated persons
  • Research on conditions particularly affecting prisoners as a class
  • Studies of therapies likely to benefit the prisoner
  • HIV/AIDS & multiple drug-resistant tuberculosis studies conducted under these conditions
2.1.11 Irony of Policy Shift
  • Historian Jon Harkness: no contemporary social consensus on prison research
  • Retrospective consensus formed only after DHEW banned it for administrative reasons
  • Paradox: intuition about exploitation may not match historical facts
  • African-American prisoners were underrepresented in most post-WWII research
  • Participation considered a privilege afforded mainly to white convicts
  • Changed only with success of civil rights movement
  • By 1960s: untoward inducements (time towards parole, high reimbursement) were being significantly curtailed
2.1.12 Belmont Principles & Prison Research
  • Even if coercion resolved & participation aids rehabilitation --> still a fatal flaw
  • Prisoners have played disproportionate role in research wherever permitted
  • Use would normally be unethical regardless of other ethical aspects
2.2 Institutionalized Persons
  • "Institutionalized" = chronically dependent on professional care (vs. brief/episodic dependence)
  • Particular concern: cognitively impaired or mentally ill persons
2.2.1 WWII Era Studies
  • Federal Committee on Medical Research (White House Office of Scientific Research & Development)
  • Approved use of asylum patients in Mississippi for influenza studies
2.2.2 1967 Pappworth Case
  • British physician H.M. Pappworth described ethically suspect experiments
  • Study example: blood flow in brains of 105 elderly demented patients
  • Insertion of two long needles into each jugular vein
  • Third needle in femoral artery of groin
  • Inhaling of radioactive gas
  • Published in major journals (British Medical Journal, Journal of Clinical Investigation)
  • Indicated research with cognitively impaired persons was common and accepted
2.2.3 Drug-Free/Washout Studies Controversy
  • Schizophrenic patients taken off psychoactive medications
  • Purpose: establish baseline behavior & assess new drug effects
  • Public attention after patient suicide at UCLA (2 years prior to investigation)
  • OPRR investigation: found nothing unethical in conduct
  • Criticism: consent form failed to clearly indicate schizophrenic symptoms may recur
2.2.4 Regulatory Gap
  • Federal regulations codified for prisoners in 1981
  • No federal regulations concerning adults with diminished decision-making capacity
  • Area remains unsettled for mentally ill & those incapacitated secondary to medical conditions
2.2.5 Growing Interest in Regulation
  • Public interest building for revisiting regulation of "decisionally impaired" research subjects
  • Driving factor: growing promise of interventions in Alzheimer's disease & associated dementias
  • Argument: varying degrees of capacity should not exclude from best therapeutic hope (research)
  • At least two sets of ethics guidelines suggested for this population
2.2.6 Debate Over Protection vs. Research Access
  • Some advocate regulation enabling research to proceed with greater confidence
  • Others emphasize risks of strategies like "drug holidays" (withdrawal of psychoactive medications)
  • Difference may stem from specific study population
  • Greater support for research in Alzheimer's disease
  • Less support for psychiatric diseases like schizophrenia
2.3 Institutionalized Children
  • Double captivity: dependent on others' care + legally/practically incapable of meaningful decisions
  • Decisions to permit participation --> parent or legal guardian (frequently the state)
2.3.1 Historical Examples
  • 1759: Francis Home (Scottish physician) --> protected 12 children from measles
  • Inoculated with blood from measles patient
  • Promised payment to parents
  • Late 1700s: Edward Jenner tested smallpox vaccine on his 1-year-old son
  • Early 1800s: institutionalized children used to test Jenner's vaccine
  • 1802: Thomas C. James inoculated 48 children in Philadelphia almshouse
2.3.2 19th Century Research Sites
  • Growing interest in childhood diseases found ready sites in:
  • Schools, orphanages, reformatories, foundling homes
  • Studies conducted for: pertussis, pellagra, STDs, scarlet fever, diphtheria, tuberculosis, chickenpox, mumps, whooping cough
2.3.3 Turn of Century Technologies
  • New technologies applied to basic physiology of children
  • X-rays for internal organ investigation
  • Stomach tubes for digestion research
2.3.4 Early 20th Century Public Suspicion
  • Changing attitudes toward children heightened public suspicion of research practices
  • 1914: Rockefeller Institute scientist used orphans in syphilis test trials
  • NY Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Children filed complaint with District Attorney
  • Physicians admitted they lacked authority to give consent
  • Charges dropped
  • Calls to outlaw "vivisectionism" in children --> proposed laws in US Senate & several state legislatures
  • None passed
2.3.5 WWII Era Federal Research
  • Federal Committee on Medical Research funded studies with children as subjects
  • 1943: Ohio orphanage site for dysentery research
  • Injections of killed bacteria caused serious side effects in some children
2.3.6 Willowbrook State School Study (Late 1950s-Early 1970s)
  • Dr. Saul Krugman & NYU team conducted hepatitis research
  • Most residents: severely mentally retarded
  • Residents developed hepatitis through exposure to bodily fluids of other children
  • Krugman systematically infected newly admitted children with virus
  • Purpose: study natural history of virus & develop prophylaxis
  • Parental consent obtained
  • Criticism: those agreeing to research subjects granted more rapid admission
  • Profoundly disabled children
  • Scholarly opinion about ethics remains unsettled
  • Krugman issued spirited defense of methods
  • One incident that aroused public concern & advanced federal regulation in 1970s
2.3.7 Fernald School Cold War Study (Late 1940s-Early 1950s)
  • Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) sponsored research
  • Cooperated with Quaker Oats cereal manufacturers
  • Residents were adolescents but not as seriously disabled as Willowbrook
  • Work performed by MIT researchers
  • Trace elements of radiation introduced into meals of male residents
  • Parents told children would be in "science club" with special meals, extra milk, field trips
  • Not told radiation was involved
2.3.8 Fernald Investigations & Findings
  • 1994: Massachusetts Task Force on Human Subject Research concluded:
  • Researchers did not provide information critical to informed decisions
  • 1995: ACHRE concluded:
  • Fernald research & similar project at Wrentham School
  • "unfairly burdened children who were already disadvantaged
  • Children whose interests were less well protected than those living with parents or socially privileged children"
  • 1997: Former students agreed to $1.85 million settlement in class-action lawsuit against Quaker Oats & MIT
2.3.9 Current Pediatric Research Regulations
  • Grew out of Willowbrook & other cases revelations
  • National Commission's recommendations became template for current rules
  • Regulations relatively detailed but give wide latitude to parents, investigators, IRBs
  • "Sliding scale" approach: restrictions vary by ratio of risk & benefit
  • Most difficult: research involving significant risk without prospect of direct benefit to subject
  • Some work exempt (e.g., anonymous educational test results)
  • Most problematic concept: "minimal risk"
  • Defined as not exceeding daily life or regular physical/psychological examination
  • May not be very protective given many hazards of ordinary childhood
2.4 Military Personnel
  • Convenient: typically healthy, "normal" persons who can be followed for years
  • Question raised: extent to which consent can be truly voluntary in disciplined environment
  • Risk of disproportionate representation, especially in national security studies
2.4.1 Historical Context
  • Military officials long considered voluntariness important condition for participation
  • Term "volunteer" or "informed volunteer" used since at least 1940s
2.4.2 Walter Reed Yellow Fever Experiment (~1900)
  • Cuba
  • Obtained consent & written contracts from potential subjects
  • Contract specified some risks
  • Offered $100 in gold to Spanish workers (significant amount at time)
  • Soldiers reportedly declined compensation
  • Little opportunity to withdraw from study
  • Reed's colleagues (not Reed himself) on Yellow Fever Commission also subjected themselves to mosquito bites
  • One colleague died of infection
2.4.3 WWII Era Policies
  • Committee on Medical Research (CMR) declared uniformed personnel not to be used as "guinea pigs"
  • Significant concern: public would not be sympathetic if heroes used this way
  • However, naval personnel were forced to remain in mustard gas experiments against will
2.4.4 Post-WWII National Security Research
  • Growing view: some human experiments necessary in postwar environment
  • Focus on unconventional weapons: atomic, biological, chemical
  • Effects could not be gauged in animal studies
  • Combat implications could not be assessed with other healthy subjects
2.4.5 Cold War Atomic Test Studies
  • Early 1950s: studies of flashblindness following atomic detonations
  • Classified by Pentagon as medical experiments
  • Most other exposures to atomic battlefield considered necessary training
  • Troops near atomic test sites systematically observed
  • Filed self-reports of panic reactions near blast site
2.4.6 Nuremberg Code Adoption (1953)
  • Department of Defense adopted Nuremberg Code as policy
  • Subsequently: troops near atomic tests observed systematically
2.4.7 Consent Form Issues
  • "Release" forms filled out in some cases by troops who "volunteered" to operate closer to ground zero
  • Higher exposure to radioactivity
  • In other radiation studies involving military personnel:
  • No documentation of volunteer status except statements of superior officers
2.4.8 Atomic Soldiers at Camp Desert Rock (1951-1962)
  • Nevada training facility
  • Vast majority kept at "safe distance" from atomic blast site
  • Primary goal: learn about human factors (e.g., panic reactions on atomic battlefield)
  • Tension between national security needs & ethical considerations rarely publicly discussed
2.4.9 Mushroom Cloud Penetration Experiments
  • Air Force experiments measuring fission released by atomic blast & effects on crew members
  • Strong evidence some air force personnel eager to experience challenge and adventure
  • Others viewed job as routine
2.4.10 Implementation Failures
  • Nuremberg Code-based policy implementation --> sporadic at best
  • Confusion about scope & application
  • 1975: Army Inspector General found Army failed to comply with own rules for research with psychoactive drugs
  • Thousands of men at Fort Detrick, Maryland used in LSD experiments (1950s)
2.4.11 Supreme Court Case
  • Soldier sued US government for injuries from LSD research
  • Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in favor of government
  • Grounds: judicial branch should not undermine discipline by inquiring into military matters
  • Dissent argued: Nuremberg Code must prevail
2.4.12 Modern Military Research
  • Reduced dependence on healthy, "normal" subjects
  • Very low threshold of risk tolerance for new armaments, equipment, materials
  • 1991: Department of Defense regulations brought under same requirements as other federal agencies
2.4.13 Current Approval Obstacles
  • Among most difficult populations from which to obtain subjects today
  • All research at Army's infectious disease institute (Fort Detrick) governed by several regulations
  • Proposals involving significant risk must be reviewed by:
  • Local IRB
  • Human Use Review and Regulatory Affairs Division (US Army Medical Research & Material Command)
  • Human Subjects Research Review Board (Office of Surgeon General)
  • Office of the Surgeon General itself
2.4.14 Clinton Administration Reforms (1997)
  • Following ACHRE recommendations
  • President Clinton ordered expanded training for senior officers on human subjects research nature
  • New policy: precludes officers from involvement in recruitment of research volunteers
2.4.15 Gulf War Informed Consent Issues (1990-1991)
  • Desert Shield & Desert Storm operations
  • Concern about exposure to biological & chemical warfare agents
  • Defense Department sought amendment to FDA informed consent regulations
  • Enable determination that obtaining consent was "not feasible" under combat conditions
  • Rule published December 21, 1990
  • Upheld by courts
2.4.16 Gulf War Waiver Products
  • Pentagon requested & received waivers for two investigational products:
  • Pyridostigmine bromide (PB)
  • Botulinum toxoid (BT)
  • Waiver obtained for both agents
  • Central Command ethical decision:
  • Gave service personnel choice about receiving BT
  • Did not give choice for PB (common use as approved drug, consent deemed unnecessary)
  • Pentagon estimates:
  • ~8000 troops took BT
  • ~250,000 received at least one dose of PB
2.4.17 Gulf War Syndrome Controversy
  • Months after war: veterans complained of numerous symptoms ("Gulf War Syndrome")
  • Vaccination program shrouded in secrecy (to deny information to enemy)
  • Agents, especially PB, theorized as factor in veterans' medical problems
  • Federal advisory committee appointed to investigate health problems & waiver process
2.4.18 Ethical Analysis of Desert Storm Drug Use
  • Argument for access to unapproved compounds under combat conditions:
  • May be ethical if technical/bureaucratic factors delayed approval
  • Sound scientific evidence that agent could significantly benefit troops in battle
  • Underlying criticism: suspicion of deliberate effort to circumvent research requirements
  • No evidence this was the case
  • Shortcoming: no system in place to document response to medications
  • Failure to establish appropriate baseline measures of subjects' metabolism
2.4.19 Research Justification Argument
  • Use "in theater" could theoretically be justified on scientific & beneficent grounds
  • If operation treated as research study according to established methodological standards
  • Had systematic research dimension been part of use:
  • Opportunity to assess fairness of conducting with military personnel
  • Assessment would turn on manner in which study was conducted
  • Soldiers facing combat conditions may be required to accept medical interventions ensuring availability for service
  • But innovative use of drugs may not entail requirement to accept them
2.4.20 Informed Consent Failure
  • Apparently information not made available in Desert Storm
  • Despite agreement between Defense Department & FDA that it would be provided
2.5 Students
  • Captive in different sense: not literally captive, often privileged
  • Characterized by inherently lesser power than teacher/relationship partner
  • Not unique: employers/employees, supervisors/laboratory workers share similar dynamics
2.5.1 Potentially Coercive Elements
  • Course requirement to serve as study subject
  • Response to campus/local advertisements offering cash for volunteering
  • Often unemployed or underemployed --> even small monetary inducements important
2.5.2 Research Types
  • Most likely exposed to behavioral research with minimal physical risk
  • Though some psychological risk possible
  • No great scandal about participation as course requirement --> least attention among captive populations
2.5.3 Deception Research
  • Social psychological studies involving deception increased greatly through 1950s & 1960s
  • Few expressed concern until mid-1960s following Stanley Milgram's obedience studies
2.5.4 Milgram Obedience Studies
  • Basic design: two people told participating in memory experiment
  • One was "confederate" (research team member)
  • Naive actual subject instructed to shock other "subject" for wrong answers
  • Believed shocks were dangerous
  • Experimenter instructed subjects to follow through on punishment for mistakes
  • Most actual subjects gave confederates "shocks" because instructed by authority figure (scientist)
2.5.5 Ethical Debate After Milgram
  • Scientific importance vied for attention with ethical issues
  • Critics concerned about emotional well-being of subjects:
  • Once realized they had been deceived
  • And that they were capable of inflicting harm on innocent people merely because instructed by authority
  • No informed consent about this aspect --> hard to obtain without confounding study
2.5.6 Laud Humphreys Tearoom Trade Study (Late 1960s)
  • Sociologist studied anonymous homosexual encounters in public restrooms
  • Data-gathering: secretly recorded car license numbers
  • Later presented himself at subjects' homes posing as health services researcher
  • Asked questions about personal lives
  • Succeeded in undermining numerous false stereotypes about gay men
  • Approach caused national newspaper uproar beyond department & university
2.5.7 APA Ethics Code
  • Continues to permit deception in research
  • Does not address disproportionate use of "captive" populations (e.g., those required as course subjects)
2.5.8 Advanced Student Researchers
  • Students engaged in advanced biological/medical studies
  • Considered close to ideal candidates due to potential intellectual identification with research
  • Only superior subjects: principal investigators themselves
2.5.9 Institutional Paternalism Argument
  • Creating special obstacles for these students (considered "best and brightest") may be viewed as paternalistic
  • Less likely to be exploited than other societal groups
2.5.10 Medical Student Skepticism
  • Evidence: medical students do not believe their professors' consent processes are adequate
2.5.11 Financial Compensation Guidelines
  • To avoid appearing coercive, remuneration should consider financial position of population
  • Students often live on loans presenting significant burden for many years
  • Compensation considerations:
  • First: expenses associated with participation (e.g., travel)
  • Additional amounts based on reasonable assessment of time value
  • Example: $100/hour for someone who could not otherwise earn fraction of that amount --> appears coercive
3. Future Trends & Predictions
3.1 Mentally Infirm Research Protection
  • Likely candidate for new/expanded regulatory protections
  • Includes: chronic cognitive deficits (Alzheimer's, schizophrenia) or minors with deficits beyond immaturity
  • Recent legal case: NY State psychiatric hospital regulations invalidated for greater than minimal risk nonbeneficial research
  • Uncertainty among investigators over consent procedures has caught attention of National Bioethics Advisory Commission (NBAC)
  • Expectation: any explicit regulations will create more obstacles to use
  • Locales where much psychiatric research done with patients --> expect fewer studies or patients in future
3.2 Military Research During Peacetime
  • General reluctance to use military personnel in research when others available (political & moral reasons)
  • Reluctance compromised when:
  • New threat seemed imminent
  • Other appropriate subjects not available
  • Future tension source: suspected new deadly weapons system in foreign power or terrorist group
  • Combined with regulatory restrictions on use of other healthy subjects
3.3 Student Research Restrictions
  • Isolated tragedies can excite considerable public alarm despite rarity of harm
  • Some further restrictions likely, at least locally
  • Possibly prohibiting recruitment by current instructors
  • 1996: University of Rochester undergraduate (19 years old) died after participating in bronchoscopy study
  • Reacted to local anesthetic --> died 2 days later
  • Was to be paid $150 as normal volunteer
  • Although harm extremely rare & mortality virtually unheard of --> case excited concern in New York
  • State health commissioner appointed panel to review use of normal subjects & recommend IRB improvements
4. Conclusions
  • Generalized discussions about justice limited for specific groups
  • Historical & practical factors vary depending on population being considered
  • Prisoners, institutionalized persons, military personnel, students --> quite different situations
  • Require analyses tailored to each
4.1 Evolution of Protectionist Stance
  • Prisoners: no longer rich source of subjects; specific federal regulations greatly restrict involvement
  • Institutionalized persons: long generated specific ethical issues --> trend recently accelerated
  • Military personnel: always sensitive problem for defense officials; must navigate numerous obstacles for command approval
  • Students, employees, others in differential power positions: simmering issue likely next frontier for protectionist approaches
4.1.1 Historical Experience & Justice Evolution
  • Accompanied by evolution in sense of justice in research
  • Tended to qualify crude utilitarian attitudes toward use of human subjects
4.1.2 Prison Debt to Society Notion
  • Once-popular notion of justice: long-term prisoners owe special debt expressible in research participation
  • Resonance only if abstracted from actual abuses associated with imprisonment (familiar problem of voluntariness)
4.1.3 Risky Studies for Important Public Health
  • View that prisoners or institutionalized persons may need to be used must be tempered by condition:
  • Already in current regulations --> they must themselves likely benefit from such research
  • Either as individuals or at minimum as members of affected group
4.1.4 Refined Justice Conception Implications
  • Once more refined conception of justice in research becomes available --> implications for groups not originally addressed
  • Example: military service does not include duties to be in research not improving combat readiness
  • Armed forces already accepting this by mid-1970s
  • Tuskegee Syphilis Study scandal & National Commission work reinforced awareness of research ethics in military
4.1.5 Student/Employee Research Stance
  • Modern conception of justice in research: proposition that role does not generate obligation to serve in experiment --> now becoming more obvious
4.2 Protectionism Does Not Rule Out Participation
  • Circumstances exist where justice may permit or even require access to research for historically abused populations
  • One circumstance: prevalence of disease posing particular threat to members of that population
  • Cannot be studied as effectively with other subjects
4.3 Protected Status Meaning
  • Implies institutional & public scrutiny of proposed research participation
  • Not a priori exclusion
4.4 Final Statement on Moral Presumption
  • With understanding of historical factors making these groups' participation in medical research matter of special concern
  • Protectionism continues to be a morally sound presumption
